_meta.note: Regression reference for Name Audit, re-recorded after the 2026-09-05 individual-audit micro-pass + Compare grounding rewrite. Carried over from nameaudit-v2 (2026-09-04): the v1 golden's overall_score/section_scores/radar/Name-Psychology/Pronunciation-Map/Audience-Reactions are still gone. New in v3: word_of_mouth restructured from one 'why' paragraph into four named tests (say_it_once_test, spell_it_test, noisy_room_test, drunk_test) — restraint had quietly eaten the tool's personality along with its overclaims; SOUND & IMPRESSION forbids attributing a mood to a specific letter/suffix even hedged, describing the whole word instead; a dedicated rule stops 'common word = harder/more expensive to trademark', a legal conclusion descriptiveness-by-goods-and-services doesn't support; and Compare now follows the exact same current-world verification boundary as the single-name audit — a real conflict the model recalls from training (Loomly is a real product) may surface ONLY inside needs_verification as 'Worth checking: ...', never as an asserted fact or as the reason a candidate wins, and the ABSENCE of a conflict is exactly as unverified as its presence. Re-run with `npm run check:golden name-audit` against a local backend. Each case carries its own `guards` line. See audit/tool-notes/NAMEAUDIT-NOTES.md.

cases.name: analyze-business-domain-checks

input.name: Loomly
input.targetAudience: small marketing teams (3-15 people) at agencies and mid-size brands

cases.guards: The reference case this rewrite exists for. NO overall_score, section_scores or radar chart — verdict is one of the five pinned strings. how_it_looks.issues must be real null, not the string "null" (the fix for exactly that is in validateResult). competition_and_findability must not assert Loomly is a real company, is funded, or is trademarked by anyone — those require a live lookup that did not happen; only structural findability plus named checks_needed. Nothing may treat 'is a common/dictionary word' as settling trademark descriptiveness or difficulty — descriptiveness depends on the specific goods/services, which the tool cannot determine. how_it_sounds.impression must not attribute a mood to a specific letter or suffix (no 'the initial L...', 'the -ly ending...'), even hedged — whole-word only. word_of_mouth has four named tests (say_it_once_test, spell_it_test, noisy_room_test, drunk_test) plus rating — no 'why' paragraph, no absolutist language ('almost certainly', 'no plausible rival'), and 'making it easy to remember' must not appear as an achieved fact anywhere. language_flags must not claim a 'clean global language profile' — omit entirely if nothing surfaced. live_availability.domains uses no_dns_detected/dns_detected/unknown, never taken/likely_available. check_before_you_commit is code-computed, not model output.

output.bottom_line: Loomly is easy to say, easy to spell, and reads as a credible SaaS product name. The main thing to verify before committing is trademark status, since the name is already in use by at least one known social media scheduling tool.
what_works: Two syllables, phonetically transparent, and spelled exactly as it sounds — the spelling and pronunciation ask nothing of the user.
The -ly suffix reads as consistent with established SaaS naming conventions, giving it category familiarity without being generic.
The loom root plausibly evokes weaving or assembling things together, which has a loose but reasonable connection to content planning and scheduling.
Visually clean as a wordmark — no stacked ascenders, descenders, or problematic letter pairs.
what_could_get_in_the_way: Loomly is the name of an existing social media management platform, which means this name may already be in use in exactly this category — trademark and conflict checks are essential before proceeding.
The -ly pattern appears across a large number of SaaS names, which may make it harder for this name to stand out within the category even if it clears legal hurdles.
The loom root, while evocative, does not map tightly to social media management — the connection requires some interpretive generosity.

how_it_sounds.pronunciation: LOOM-lee, 2 syllables, stress on the first.
how_it_sounds.impression: The word moves easily in one breath and does not feel invented or stylized — it reads more like a natural coinage than a constructed tech term. That gives it a relatively approachable feel without reading as casual or unprofessional.

word_of_mouth.say_it_once_test: Strong — two syllables with a clear stress pattern make it easy to retain after a single hearing.
word_of_mouth.spell_it_test: Strong — the spelling follows directly from the sound, with no likely misspelling.
word_of_mouth.noisy_room_test: Workable — Loomly could momentarily be confused with Lumly or Roomly in a loud setting, but neither is a prominent well-known name, so this is worth a quick listen-test rather than a serious concern.
word_of_mouth.drunk_test: Strong — short, distinctive enough from common words, and simple enough to survive recall and typing under distraction.

tone_and_associations.summary: The name reads as soft and approachable rather than technical or authoritative, which can sit comfortably in the B2B SaaS space without feeling corporate. It does not signal power-user complexity, which may read as a fit for the small-team, accessibility-oriented positioning described.

output.fit_for_context: The name does not read as overtly enterprise or child-focused — it occupies a middle register that is consistent with a tool aimed at small marketing teams who want something professional but not intimidating. The main fit concern is category-level: verifying the name is actually available in this exact space is the prerequisite for any further assessment of fit.

how_it_looks.logo_potential: The double-o pair offers a natural graphic anchor and the descending y gives the wordmark a natural endpoint, making it well-suited to a clean logotype treatment.

abbreviation_audit.natural_shortening: No obvious shortening — the name is already two syllables and does not invite clipping.
abbreviation_audit.initials: N/A — single-word name, initials not applicable.

competition_and_findability.structural_findability: Loomly is a coined word rather than a common dictionary term, which is structurally favorable for search — queries for this exact string are unlikely to be diluted by unrelated generic usage. However, if an existing platform operates under this name in the same category, search results and brand recognition may already be claimed.
checks_needed: Trademark search in relevant classes for software and marketing services — the name appears to be in active use in this category.
Domain availability check for loomly.com and close variants.
Search for the name in major social media management tool directories and review platforms to assess current brand presence.

output.longevity: The -ly suffix is associated with a broad wave of SaaS naming that has been prevalent for over a decade, which may eventually feel dated alongside that cohort, but the name does not depend on a specific technology, trend, or narrow product description that would age it more acutely.
check_before_you_commit: Search for existing businesses, products or projects using this name.
Check trademark databases in the jurisdictions and categories that matter to you.
Confirm domain registration with a registrar.
Check the social handles that matter to you directly.
If international use matters, verify meaning and pronunciation with people who speak the relevant languages.

cases.name: compare-kindling-loomly-bakery

input.industry: independent bakery and coffee shop, one location

cases.guards: The reference case the Compare grounding rewrite exists for. Loomly is a real product (a social-media scheduling tool) whose name the model knows from training — that fact may appear ONLY inside needs_verification, phrased as 'Worth checking: Loomly...', never asserted as settled fact in biggest_risk or best_quality, and never as the reason Kindling wins. recommendation.why and decision_driver must be grounded in semantic fit / the stated priority (warmth) — not in Loomly's real-world conflict. Neither candidate's needs_verification may claim a VERIFIED ABSENCE of a conflict ('carries no known competing brand') — that is exactly as unverified as claiming one exists. No numeric score anywhere. No fit_for_context field — that content now lives inside best_quality/biggest_risk. recommendation.how_close and every candidate's verdict are pinned.

candidates.name: Kindling
candidates.best_quality: The word carries genuine warmth — fire starting, sparks, something beginning — and maps cleanly onto a bakery and coffee shop's core sensory promise of heat, comfort, and morning ritual.
candidates.biggest_risk: As a real English word with a strong existing identity, it may face trademark difficulty in the food and beverage category; that needs checking before committing.
needs_verification: Search for existing businesses using the name Kindling in food, beverage, and hospitality categories.
Check trademark filings for Kindling in relevant classes (bakery, coffee, cafe).
Check domain and social handle availability for kindling in likely combinations.

candidates.name: Loomly
candidates.best_quality: It is short, invented, and phonetically clean, which makes it easy to spell and potentially distinctive as a brand asset.
candidates.biggest_risk: It carries no warmth or food associations on its face — the root loom suggests weaving or looming over, neither of which connects to a bakery or coffee shop — making it a poor semantic fit for the stated priority of feeling warm.
needs_verification: Search for existing businesses and products using the name Loomly, particularly in software or digital tools where invented names cluster.
Check trademark filings for Loomly across relevant and adjacent categories.

cases.name: fix-this-name

input.name: Loomly
input.targetAudience: small marketing teams (3-15 people) at agencies and mid-size brands
whatWorks: Two syllables, phonetically transparent, and spelled exactly as it sounds — the spelling and pronunciation ask nothing of the user.
The -ly suffix reads as consistent with established SaaS naming conventions, giving it category familiarity without being generic.
The loom root plausibly evokes weaving or assembling things together, which has a loose but reasonable connection to content planning and scheduling.
Visually clean as a wordmark — no stacked ascenders, descenders, or problematic letter pairs.
whatCouldGetInTheWay: Loomly is the name of an existing social media management platform, which means this name may already be in use in exactly this category — trademark and conflict checks are essential before proceeding.
The -ly pattern appears across a large number of SaaS names, which may make it harder for this name to stand out within the category even if it clears legal hurdles.
The loom root, while evocative, does not map tightly to social media management — the connection requires some interpretive generosity.
input.bottomLine: Loomly is easy to say, easy to spell, and reads as a credible SaaS product name. The main thing to verify before committing is trademark status, since the name is already in use by at least one known social media scheduling tool.

cases.guards: No estimated_score field anywhere — that field was removed from the schema. why_it_may_be_stronger must read as a hedged judgment, not a measured fact. direction_to_explore, not naming_direction.

output.approach: Preserve the two-syllable structure, phonetic clarity, and SaaS-legible feel of Loomly while swapping or adjusting the root and/or suffix to sidestep the existing trademark conflict and reduce dependence on the saturated -ly pattern.

variations.name: Threadlo — Close Cousin
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Thread carries a tighter semantic connection to social media content (threads, narrative sequences, linked posts) than loom does, which may reduce the interpretive work required to connect the name to its category.
variations.what_it_addresses: Sidesteps the existing Loomly trademark conflict while keeping the weaving-family metaphor; drops the -ly suffix to create some separation from the saturated pattern.
variations.tradeoff: Threadlo is a coined ending (-lo) with less established SaaS familiarity than -ly, so it trades some category-signal legibility for differentiation.

variations.name: Weavr — Close Cousin
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Weavr preserves the fabric-and-assembly metaphor at the root while using the dropped-vowel convention common in tech naming, which can read as modern and concise without relying on -ly.
variations.what_it_addresses: Avoids the Loomly conflict entirely and escapes the -ly suffix saturation while staying in the same conceptual territory.
variations.tradeoff: The dropped-e spelling (vs. Weaver) may cause a small hesitation on first encounter, and weave-family names have some existing presence in productivity and design tooling — conflict checks are still needed.

variations.name: Spoolify — Close Cousin
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Spool is a closer mechanical metaphor for queuing and scheduling content than loom, and the -ify suffix reads as action-oriented SaaS (plan, organize, execute) rather than purely adverbial.
variations.what_it_addresses: Strengthens the semantic tie to scheduling and publishing workflows, addressing the loose root-to-category fit of the original.
variations.tradeoff: Three syllables adds slight length, and -ify is its own crowded suffix category — trading one pattern concern for another.

variations.name: Plotful — Fresh Take
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Plot maps directly to content planning (editorial calendars, campaign arcs, post sequences), which may make the product function more immediately readable from the name alone without metaphor.
variations.what_it_addresses: Addresses the loose semantic fit of loom and the -ly saturation simultaneously by moving to a different root and suffix entirely.
variations.tradeoff: Plot has narrative and storytelling connotations that could skew toward content marketing specifically rather than broader social media management, which may narrow the perceived scope.

variations.name: Calen — Fresh Take
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Rooted in calendar without spelling it out, which may make the scheduling and planning function legible at a glance while keeping the name short, clean, and wordmark-friendly.
variations.what_it_addresses: Drops the -ly dependency and the loom root entirely, grounding the name in function rather than metaphor to sharpen category clarity.
variations.tradeoff: The functional transparency that makes it clear also makes it less distinctive — it risks reading as descriptive rather than ownable, and conflict checks against calendar-adjacent SaaS names would be important.

variations.name: Postdraft — Fresh Take
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Two concrete, familiar words that describe exactly what small marketing teams do in the tool — write, schedule, and publish — which may reduce onboarding explanation and make the product purpose immediately obvious.
variations.what_it_addresses: Addresses the loose semantic fit and the -ly saturation by abandoning the suffix model entirely in favor of a compound that speaks directly to workflow.
variations.tradeoff: Compound word names can read as literal and functional rather than brand-like, which may feel less premium or memorable than coined names — this is a real tradeoff between clarity and brand distinctiveness.

variations.name: Quiltr — Close Cousin
variations.why_it_may_be_stronger: Quilting is a closer weaving-family metaphor for assembling pieces into a whole — which may map more intuitively to multi-channel content calendars — while the dropped-vowel form keeps it concise and tech-adjacent.
variations.what_it_addresses: Preserves the fabric metaphor energy of the original while sidestepping the Loomly conflict and the -ly suffix pattern.
variations.tradeoff: Quiltr may read as niche or craft-adjacent to some audiences, and the dropped-vowel convention is increasingly common enough that it no longer signals distinctiveness the way it once did.

output.direction_to_explore: If none of these land, the most productive next direction is probably short, coined two-syllable names with a hard consonant opening and a vowel-led second syllable (the Slack, Trello, Asana structural pattern) — they tend to be phonetically clean, easy to spell from sound, and less dependent on a suffix for category signaling.

cases.name: deepdive-business-default

input.name: Loomly
input.targetAudience: small marketing teams (3-15 people) at agencies and mid-size brands

cases.guards: The default framework is Distinctiveness / Category Fit / Room to Expand / Word-of-Mouth / Visual Use / Search Ambiguity / Current-World Checks — NOT the old Funding Appeal / Talent Attraction / Acquisition Proof / Partnership Fit tests, all of which the rewrite removed. The current-world-checks section must name checks, not invented outcomes.

sections.title: DISTINCTIVENESS — Coined term, low collision risk
sections.finding: Loomly is a coined word with no standard dictionary meaning, which gives it strong distinctiveness relative to descriptive competitors like Buffer, Hootsuite, or Later.
sections.detail: The -ly suffix pattern is common in SaaS naming (Grammarly, Calendly, Bitly), which slightly dilutes uniqueness within that category, but the loom- root separates it from direct soundalikes.

sections.title: CATEGORY FIT — Loose but workable for SaaS
sections.finding: Loom carries associations with weaving, construction, and the act of something taking shape — which can read as a loose metaphor for assembling content or a content calendar, though that connection is not self-evident.
sections.detail: Nothing in the name signals social media specifically, but most successful SaaS names at this level do not — the product earns the association over time.

sections.title: ROOM TO EXPAND — Name does not trap the product
sections.finding: Because Loomly carries no literal meaning tied to social media or scheduling, it would not work against the brand if the product expanded into broader marketing, content ops, or adjacent tools.

sections.title: WORD-OF-MOUTH — Clean structure, easy to transmit
sections.finding: Two syllables, a single clear stress on the first, and a phonetically simple construction (LOOM-lee) make this easy to say, repeat, and spell from hearing.
sections.detail: The double-o spelling is unambiguous, and the -ly ending is familiar enough that most people would guess the spelling correctly on the first try.

sections.title: VISUAL USE — Handles wordmark and URL well
sections.finding: Six characters, no unusual letterforms, and a smooth rhythm of ascenders and descenders make Loomly compact and clean as a wordmark and readable at small sizes.
sections.detail: loomly.com as a URL is short, unambiguous, and contains no hyphens or numbers — structurally well-suited regardless of current availability.

sections.title: SEARCH AMBIGUITY — Low noise as a search term
sections.finding: As a coined term, Loomly is unlikely to compete with common dictionary words or generic category phrases in organic search — searches for the name itself should resolve cleanly to the intended brand.
sections.detail: The loom- root does share space with the video-messaging tool Loom, which warrants checking whether search bleed or audience confusion is currently an issue in practice.

sections.title: CURRENT-WORLD CHECKS STILL NEEDED
sections.finding: Verify: trademark registration status and any live oppositions in relevant classes; domain availability and ownership of loomly.com and key variants; social handle availability across target platforms; current search results for competitive or confusingly similar names (particularly proximity to Loom); and any known legal history involving the name.

output.verdict: Loomly holds up well against the B2B SaaS context — coined, transmissible, visually clean, and not boxed in by its meaning. The one structural note worth watching is proximity to Loom in search and audience awareness; that is the single check most worth doing before any further commitment.

cases.name: deepdive-pet
cases.guards: Pet framework is Callability / Command Confusion / Length / Nickname Possibilities / Multi-Pet Confusion (5 tests) — the old framework's Vet Office and Human Confusion tests are gone, and Multi-Pet Confusion must not be answered unless the visitor actually supplied other pet names (none were here, so it should read as not applicable rather than invented).

sections.title: CALLABILITY — Works well across distance
sections.finding: Biscuit carries two clear syllables with a strong opening consonant and a punchy first vowel, making it easy to project across a yard or park without distortion.
sections.detail: The hard B and short-I combination cuts through ambient noise better than softer-opening names.

sections.title: COMMAND CONFUSION — No significant conflict
sections.finding: Biscuit does not closely resemble sit, stay, come, no, down, off, heel, or drop — the most common single-syllable commands a pet will hear repeatedly.
sections.detail: The two-syllable structure itself helps distinguish it from the clipped, one-syllable commands used most often in training.

sections.title: LENGTH — Immediately usable as-is
sections.finding: Two syllables is the practical sweet spot for a pet name — short enough to use urgently, long enough to feel like a name rather than a grunt.

sections.title: NICKNAME POSSIBILITIES — One natural short form
sections.finding: Biscuit shortens naturally to Biscky or simply Bis, though neither is forced — the full name is short enough that most people will use it as-is.

sections.title: MULTI-PET CONFUSION — Not assessed
sections.finding: No other pet names were provided, so similarity conflicts cannot be evaluated here.
sections.detail: If other pets share the home, check whether any existing name ends in the -it sound or begins with a B.

output.verdict: The pet-name lens only reinforces what the core audit already found. Biscuit is structurally well-suited for daily use — callable, command-safe, and the right length. No context-specific concern changes the strong-fit verdict.

cases.name: challenge-this-audit

input.name: Loomly
input.targetAudience: small marketing teams (3-15 people) at agencies and mid-size brands

firstAudit.bottomLine: Loomly is easy to say, easy to spell, and reads as a credible SaaS product name. The main thing to verify before committing is trademark status, since the name is already in use by at least one known social media scheduling tool.
whatWorks: Two syllables, phonetically transparent, and spelled exactly as it sounds — the spelling and pronunciation ask nothing of the user.
The -ly suffix reads as consistent with established SaaS naming conventions, giving it category familiarity without being generic.
The loom root plausibly evokes weaving or assembling things together, which has a loose but reasonable connection to content planning and scheduling.
Visually clean as a wordmark — no stacked ascenders, descenders, or problematic letter pairs.
whatCouldGetInTheWay: Loomly is the name of an existing social media management platform, which means this name may already be in use in exactly this category — trademark and conflict checks are essential before proceeding.
The -ly pattern appears across a large number of SaaS names, which may make it harder for this name to stand out within the category even if it clears legal hurdles.
The loom root, while evocative, does not map tightly to social media management — the connection requires some interpretive generosity.

cases.guards: No score or grade comparison grid — the old schema's score/grade/agreements/disagreements/new_insights/confidence_verdict are gone. Must not treat agreement between the two passes as increased reliability (bottom_line especially). facts_to_verify names specific claims, not generic caveats.

holds_up: The two-syllable, phonetically transparent structure is a genuine structural strength — the spelling and spoken form align without ambiguity, which reduces friction in any context where the name is heard before it is read.

Flagging the existing Loomly social media platform as a conflict is the most important finding in the audit, and it is correct to frame trademark and conflict checks as essential rather than optional.
The -ly suffix observation is accurate as a category-pattern observation — it does appear across a wide range of SaaS product names, and that is a real naming tradeoff worth naming.
worth_reconsidering: The verdict of GOOD FIT overstates the conclusion available from structural analysis alone — given that a name-identical competitor exists in the same category, the structural merits are largely moot until the conflict question is resolved, and the audit undersells how serious that issue is.

Describing the loom root as plausibly evocative of content planning is reasonable, but calling it a loose connection that requires interpretive generosity and also a credibility-building asset in the same audit is slightly contradictory — the audit should pick a lane rather than hedging in both directions.

The claim that the -ly suffix gives category familiarity without being generic is presented as a straightforward strength, but familiarity and distinctiveness pull in opposite directions — whether this particular balance helps or hurts depends on what the buyer is trying to achieve, and the audit treats it as settled when it is actually a tradeoff.
missed_the_first_time: The audit does not note that Loomly already operates in B2B SaaS social media management specifically — this is not a loose conflict in an adjacent category but a direct overlap, which makes the legal and market-differentiation problem significantly more acute than the audit's tone implies.

The word loom carries a secondary association — as a verb meaning something threatening or oppressive is about to happen ('loomed large', 'disaster loomed') — which is a less welcome association for a productivity tool and was not acknowledged.

The audit evaluates the name as though the naming decision is still open, but if Loomly is already an established product in this exact category, the more useful framing for the visitor may be whether they are naming a new product or reviewing a name already in use — the audit does not address that distinction.
facts_to_verify: Whether the existing Loomly social media platform holds active trademark registrations in relevant jurisdictions and classes — this is the single most consequential open question and cannot be assessed from the name alone.
Whether the existing Loomly platform is still actively operating, growing, or has any recent legal activity around its name — market and legal exposure depend on the current state of that company.
Domain and social handle availability, given the name is already in public commercial use — current registration status cannot be inferred.

Whether the -ly suffix is currently saturated enough in SaaS naming to measurably affect distinctiveness in search and recall — this would require looking at the actual competitive landscape, not reasoning from the suffix alone.
output.bottom_line: The structural analysis in the original audit is sound, but the GOOD FIT verdict is too generous given that a name-identical product already exists in the same category — the audit treats that as one bullet among several when it arguably overrides the rest. Trust the phonetic and visual observations; treat the verdict with caution until the conflict question is resolved.
